summary.value: This paper introduces a lifelong learning setting for the VRP domain and proposes the Lifelong Learning Router with Behavior Consolidation (LLR-BC) to address the issue of catastrophic forgetting. Specifically, LLR-BC incorporates Confidence-aware Experience Weighting (CaEW) to prioritize critical experiences and Decision-seeking Behavior Consolidation (DsBC) to emphasize replicating past decisions. Extensive experiments on TSP and CVRP benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of LLR-BC.

strengths.value:
* The paper is overall well-written and easy to follow.
* The studied topic, i.e., generalization of neural VRP solvers, is important, and the proposed setting is sound.
* The experiments are generally extensive and solid, demonstrating that the catastrophic forgetting issue is significantly mitigated, as shown in Fig. 3.

weaknesses.value:
* This paper applies lifelong learning to the VRP domain, incorporating a reweighting mechanism and reverse KL divergence. The overall technical novelty appears somewhat limited.
* In line with the no free lunch principle, while the proposed method mitigates catastrophic forgetting on previous tasks, it may incur trade-offs elsewhere. Could the authors clarify what is sacrificed or traded off in their approach or setting?
* The caption of Fig. 2 should explicitly explain all notations.

We are grateful to the reviewers for their constructive feedback, which has greatly helped us improve the clarity and quality of this work. We have revised the paper accordingly and highlighted all changes in blue. Below, we provide point-by-point responses to all comments.

**W1: This paper applies lifelong learning to the VRP domain, incorporating a reweighting mechanism and reverse KL divergence. The overall technical novelty appears somewhat limited.**

Compared with existing studies of lifelong learning in neural VRP solvers [1,2], our technical novelties in method design are as follows:
- **Formulation of experience.** We treat each step (a ⟨state, behavior⟩ pair) in solving an instance as one experience, whereas [1,2] treat the entire instance as one experience. This step-based formulation provides finer granularity and is more effective under the same computational budget. We conducted an additional ablation study (Section 4.4, Table 3) comparing LLR-BC with an instance-based variant (LLR-BC-IB), and the results confirm the superior effectiveness of our step-based design.
- **Additional cost for generating experience.** Our method reuses previously buffered experiences for consolidation instead of regenerating new ones as in [1,2]. This reduces computational cost and also makes our approach applicable to scenarios where instance generation is uncontrollable, in which **the methods of [1,2] cannot be directly applied**.
- **How consolidation is performed.** To preserve previously learned knowledge when learning a new task, [2] constrains the parameters of the current model to stay close to those of the previous model, in a way similar to EWC. As shown in experiments of our original paper (cf. Table 1), parameter-level regularization (EWC, LiBOG) leads to inferior performance. The method in [1] encourages the current and previous models to behave similarly **on the new task**. In contrast, our method encourages the current and previous models to exhibit similar behavior **on the previous tasks**. Behaviors on previous tasks encode more direct knowledge about those tasks and therefore provide more effective signals for consolidation. Our method thus achieves better performance than [1] and [2] in the following reported experiments.
- **Additional design components.** In addition, we introduce a new confidence-based weighting scheme and an new RKLD-based decision-seeking consolidation objective, as described in the original manuscript (Sections 3.2 and 3.3). The new components further improve the performance of our method (cf. Section 4.4 and Table 3 of the original paper).

Comparison with [3,4], as well as the ablation studies on experience weighting and RKLD, are already included in our original paper (cf. Tables 1 and 3). **In addition, we have adapted and implemented the methods in [1] and [2] and compared them with our approach to further verify the effectiveness of our design.** The results, shown below, demonstrate that generally our method achieves the best performance. Notably, although the methods of [1] exhibit less forgetting (AF, AMF), their plasticity (APl) for learning the new task is poor, because half of the epochs on the new task are spent learning purely from instances of previous tasks. As a result, their overall performance on seen (AP) and unseen (AG) tasks is inferior. We appreciate the reviewer’s careful reading and have revised the sentence accordingly.

**Q1: Is Fig. 1 a conceptual illustration or based on real experimental results?**

Fig. 1 is a conceptual illustration. We did not use real experimental results because (i) there are significant differences in distance scales between tasks, and (ii) fluctuations during training would hinder the clarity of the illustration.


**Q2: Could LLR-BC be applied to SL-based solvers as well?**

Yes, it can be applied to SL-based solvers with only very small adaptations: 
1. In SL there is no explicit definition of “state”. Therefore, an experience may no longer be a ⟨state, behavior⟩ pair as in RL. In general, an experience can be any ⟨model input, model output⟩ pair. The detailed definition depends on the specific design of the solver. 
2. Depending on how the model output is defined, the decision-confidence measure may need to be adapted.


**Q3: The experience buffer is state-based, why not consider an instance-based design?**

We thank the reviewer for raising this thoughtful point. With the same buffer size (in terms of buffered steps (<state, behavior> pairs) ), instance-based design reduces the instance-diversity of the buffer, potentially leading to inferior performance. We have added an ablation variant in our ablation study (cf. Section 4.4, Table 3, and Appendix C.3) that conducts instance-based experience buffering, denoted LLR-BC-IB. Specifically, LLR-BC-IB treats all steps (⟨state, behavior⟩ pairs) for solving a batch of instances (since the buffer is at the batch level) as one experience. We set the buffer size to 20 so that the expected number of buffered steps is larger than in LLR-BC (20 * $\frac{20+20+50+50+100+100}{6}$ ≈ 1133 > 1000 ). The experimental results, shown below, indicate that our state-based buffer design outperforms the instance-based buffer design, verifying the effectiveness of our design. summary.value: This paper presents a lifelong learning framework called LLR-BC for learning to solve Vehicle Routing Problems (VRPs) across different distributions and scales. LLR-BC employs a customized experience replay strategy across sequentially arising tasks to prevent catastrophic forgetting. The approach introduces two key components: a confidence-aware experience weighting (CaEW) module and a decision-seeking behavior consolidation (DsBC) loss based on reverse KL divergence. Results on TSP and CVRP validate the effectiveness of the proposed methods against baselines.

strengths.value:
* The paper studies an interesting and relatively underexplored area for neural VRP solvers: lifelong learning across diverse problem distributions and scales. 
* The presentation and illustrations are clear, making the paper easy to follow. 
* The work presents comprehensive experiments covering multiple task orders, diverse distributions and scales, and multiple backbone VRP neural solvers.
* The performance appears promising under the employed metrics.

weaknesses.value:
* There is some conceptual overlap with existing works, such as Li et al. 2024 and Feng et al. 2025, which address similar lifelong learning setups. It would be useful to directly compare with these existing methods. Also, while the customization of the replay buffer for VRPs is appreciated, the idea of experience replay is a standard technique in lifelong learning literature.
* The paper proposes using the variance of node selection probabilities as a proxy for model confidence. However, this lacks clear empirical evidence or theoretical justification that probability variance truly represents confidence. My concern is that this may be too strong and fails to distinguish between two scenarios: (1) a genuinely low-confidence model with high uncertainty, and (2) a policy that has learned multi-modal decisions where multiple nodes are equally good selections at certain division points with high confidence. 
* The design and naming regarding “DsBC” seem confusing to me, as the loss functions in Equations (1) and (2) are relatively straightforward applications of reverse KL divergence. It is unclear what new conceptual insights or contributions DsBC provides here.
* While the experiments are extensive in scope, the absolute performance of the model on each individual task is never reported. In practice, practitioners care not only about whether a lifelong learning model can avoid catastrophic forgetting, but also about the actual solution quality (such as optimality gaps) achieved on each new task. 
* The paper lacks a comparison with other state-of-the-art methods that target generalization across distributions without requiring additional training or lifelong learning mechanisms.

questions.value:
Other than the questions listed in the weakness, I also have the following questions:
* Which epoch of the model training is used to update the buffer experience, and what is the rationale for this choice? How sensitive is performance to this decision?
* How are the hyperparameters for buffer batch size determined?
* How well does variance actually serve as a proxy for confidence? Are there empirical studies or theoretical analyses that validate this design choice against alternative confidence measures?
* How diverse is the experience buffer after running the algorithm? Does the buffer maintain sufficient diversity across tasks, or does it become dominated by certain task types or distributions?

**W2: The paper proposes using the variance of node selection probabilities as a proxy for model confidence. However, this lacks clear empirical evidence or theoretical justification that probability variance truly represents confidence. My concern is that this may be too strong and fails to distinguish between two scenarios: (1) a genuinely low-confidence model with high uncertainty, and (2) a policy that has learned multi-modal decisions where multiple nodes are equally good selections at certain division points with high confidence.**


We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful comment and agree that the two scenarios raised are both possible. However, in our work we use the variance of the action probabilities as a measure of **decision confidence** for a specific state, in order to assess the importance of that state (and its corresponding experience). This is related to, but different from, the overall **model confidence**, which characterizes the model as a whole.

Evaluating state importance via the variance of action probabilities is widely used in the literature [3,4]. We follow this established practice and therefore did not provide additional empirical justification.

In LLR-BC, experiences are buffered at the last training epoch of each task, when we assume the model is already well trained on that task. Under this setting, a state with low **decision confidence** is important in either of the following two cases: (i) high uncertainty indicates that the state is difficult to learn and thus crucial for learning the task [3,4]; (ii) multiple equally good actions, which mainly lead to similarly good solutions, create plateaus in the solution space and make the optimization problem harder to solve [5,6]. Since both types of states are important and should be emphasized, it is not necessary to distinguish them in our current framework. We have added additional discussion about it in the Appendix A.4 in our revised paper. Nevertheless, inspired by the comment, we believe that explicitly differentiating and handling these two cases with more refined mechanisms is a promising direction for future work.


[3] Tamilselvan Balasuntharam, Heidar Davoudi and Mehran Ebrahimi. Preferential Proximal Policy Optimization, International Conference on Machine Learning and Applications (ICMLA), pp. 293-300, 2023. 

[4] Yitzhak Spielberg and Amos Azaria. The Concept of Criticality in Reinforcement Learning, IEEE International Conference on Tools with Artificial Intelligence (ICTAI), pp. 251-258, 2019. 

[5] Sara Tari, Matthieu Basseur and Adrien Goëffon. Sampled Walk and Binary Fitness Landscapes Exploration, Lecture Notes in Computer Science, vol 10764. 2018.

**W3: The design and naming regarding “DsBC” seem confusing to me, as the loss functions in Equations (1) and (2) are relatively straightforward applications of reverse KL divergence. It is unclear what new conceptual insights or contributions DsBC provides here.**

Beyond using RKLD as a loss to emphasize the chosen decision (decision-seeking), our Decision-seeking Behavior Consolidation (DsBC) framework also consolidates knowledge from previous tasks via buffered behaviors, i.e., ***behavior consolidation***. Specifically, we leverage the behaviors of past models that are well trained on previous tasks (before forgetting occurs) to guide the consolidation of future models. Rather than relying solely on newly generated instances from old tasks [1,2], we explicitly store the behaviors of historical policies and use them to regularize subsequent training. This design avoids repeatedly generating and solving instances from previous tasks, thereby substantially reducing computational cost and removing the need for controllable instance generation. Moreover, behaviors on previous tasks directly contain the model’s learned knowledge about those tasks, making the consolidation of prior knowledge more straightforward and effective.


In this revision, we implemented the methods in [1] and [2] and compared them against LLR-BC, and the experimental results support the performance advantages and contributions of our designs (cf. the response to **W1**). We have also revised Section 4 of the manuscript to clarify these points.

We sincerely thank the reviewer for carefully reading our previous response and for acknowledging its value. We also appreciate the additional feedback on W2 and provide further clarification below.


***"The paper proposes using the variance of node selection probabilities as a proxy for model confidence. However, this lacks clear empirical evidence or theoretical justification that probability variance truly represents confidence."***

In our work, we use the variance of node selection probabilities as a proxy for the **confidence of a specific decision**, i.e., how confident the policy model is in its selected node for a given state. To the best of our knowledge, the term *"model confidence"* is not a standard concept in the DRL literature. We therefore interpret the reviewer’s use of *"model confidence"* as referring to the **confidence of individual decisions** made by a model.

In the DRL literature, **confidence** is most commonly formalized via the **negative entropy** of the action selection probability distribution (e.g., *"'Confidence' is calculated as negative entropy"* in [1], *"we use the model’s underlying confidence (negative entropy) as a reward"* in [2], *"the negative entropy formulation ensures that lower entropy (higher confidence) receives higher reward"* in [3]). In the following, we therefore take **negative entropy** as the canonical mathematical representation of confidence and show that **variance can represent confidence (negative entropy) very well**, both theoretically and empirically.

* **Theoretical justification.** Variance and negative entropy share the same qualitative behavior as functions of the selected action probability. For clarity, we consider a binary-action case with actions $a_1$ and $a_2$. Suppose the policy outputs probabilities $p_1 = p$ and $p_2 = 1 - p$. Let $\bar{p} = \frac{p_1 + p_2}{2} = 0.5$ denote the mean probability. Then the variance and confidence (negative entropy) can be written as: $\mathrm{var}(p_1, p_2) = (p - 0.5)^2$, $\mathrm{conf}(p_1, p_2) = p \log p + (1-p)\log(1-p)$.

  * **Shared monotonic behavior.** The gradients of variance and confidence with respect to $p$ are $\frac{\partial\ \mathrm{var}}{\partial p} = 2p - 1,\quad \frac{\partial\ \mathrm{conf}}{\partial p} = \log\frac{p}{1-p}$. Both gradients are positive when $p > 0.5$ and negative when $p < 0.5$, i.e., both quantities increase as the selected action becomes more likely than all alternatives and decrease when it becomes less likely. Thus, variance and negative entropy exhibit the **same qualitative dependence on the selected action probability**.
  * **Shared minimum.** Both quantities attain their minimum at the uniform distribution $p_1 = p_2 = 0.5$, where the policy is maximally uncertain. This is exactly the situation of **lowest confidence**, and both variance and negative entropy capture it consistently.


* **Empirical evidence.** We also observe strong empirical alignment between variance and negative entropy:
  * **High correlation on buffered experiences.** We compute both the variance and the negative entropy for all experiences stored in the buffer after running LLR-BC once under task order 1. The Pearson correlation coefficient between the two measurements is **0.972367** (where 1 indicates perfect positive correlation), showing that, in practice, variance tracks confidence during the lifelong learning process very well.
  * **Similar impact on performance.** As reported in our previous response to W2, we conduct an ablation study comparing the original LLR-BC with LLR-BC-Ent (which uses negative entropy instead of variance). Their performance is very close. This supports the claim that **variance is an effective and a good proxy for confidence**.

[1] Junhyuk Oh, et al. Discovering state-of-the-art reinforcement learning algorithms. Nature, 2025. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09761-x  

[2] Mihir Prabhudesai, et al. Maximizing Confidence Alone Improves Reasoning. arXiv, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22660  

[3] Guobin Shen, et al. Safety Instincts: LLMs Learn to Trust Their Internal Compass for Self-Defense. arXiv, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01088  


***"My concern is that this may be too strong and fails to distinguish between two scenarios: (1) a genuinely low-confidence model with high uncertainty, and (2) a policy that has learned multi-modal decisions where multiple nodes are equally good selections at certain division points with high confidence."***

In our method, the **goal of the confidence measure is to quantify the importance of an experience**, thereby identifying states/behaviors that are more informative or more vulnerable to forgetting in lifelong learning. From this perspective, as discussed in our previous response, our framework does **not require** distinguishing between the two scenarios above. Both are important and should be emphasized during training, which is exactly what LLR-BC does.

Our contributions and novelties compared to [1,2] lie in two main aspects.


**1. Difference in scenarios and assumptions.** 
We consider an online lifelong learning scenario where tasks can differ in both **distribution** and **scale**, arrive in a **random and unknown order**, and must be handled sequentially. Our objective is to improve, at each time step, the solver’s performance on all learned tasks and its generalization to unseen tasks. - **Assumptions on task distribution and scale.** In [1], tasks share the same distribution (node coordinates and demand) and differ only in scale. [2] considers a scenario where tasks share the same distribution and scale but different distance metric, and also the scenario of [1]. In contrast, we do not impose these assumptions: tasks may follow different distributions and have different scales, and the information of each task is unknown until it arrives. Since distribution shifts are common in real-world applications, removing the identical-distribution-and-scale assumption makes our scenario more realistic but also more challenging. Improving neural solvers under distribution shifts is recognized as both difficult and important [3,4,5]. Accordingly, our scenario and contributions are significantly different from those of [1,2]. Consistent with this, the methods in [1,2], which are specifically designed and evaluated only in their scenarios, perform poorly in our scenario, as shown by the new experimental comparisons we added.
- **Assumptions on task order.**  Both [1] and [2] assume that the task order is fixed and known. In [1], task scales gradually increase, and their method explicitly exploits this order (“This strategy is devised to ensure that the deep model is primarily trained on the current task, i.e., the VRP with a larger size and higher complexity than the previous ones”, Section 4.1 of [1]). [2] targets a specific sequence of changes in the distance metric, and also the scenario of [1]. As task order has a strong impact on lifelong learning performance [6], this is a restrictive assumption. We instead study more general and practical scenarios where the order is random and unknown, and our method is not tailored to any particular order. Our experiments therefore use multiple randomly generated task orders for a comprehensive evaluation, and verify the superior performance of our method.
- **Assumptions on control over problem instance generation.** Both [1] and [2] assume that the learner can actively generate new training instances from previous tasks. In our scenario, the lifelong learner has no control over instance generation. Consequently, **their methods that rely on generating new problem instances for selected past tasks cannot be directly applied in our scenarios**.
- **Assessment protocol.** To match our objective, we evaluate the solver’s performance on each task both before and after training on it. By contrast, [1] and [2] mainly test and report performance only after training on all tasks, i.e., at the end of the lifelong learning process, without intermediate evaluation. Taken together with the above assumptions, [1] and [2] are closer to curriculum learning methods, which aim to obtain a strong final model under a specific training order (e.g., from easy to hard). In contrast, our work evaluates performance both during and at the end of learning, proposes a comprehensive set of metrics, and reports detailed results and analysis over the entire lifelong learning process.


The aforementioned differences in scenarios are summarized below:

| ---- | - | ------- |------- |
| [1] | scale  | fixed, scale gradually increases | Have control
| [2]   | scale or distance metric  | fixed, scale gradually increases / Euclidean→Manhattan→Chebyshev | Have control
| ours | distribution and scale  | random and unknown | No control

Dear AC,

Thank you for coordinating the review process at this stage, and we are also grateful to the previous AC for the efforts in overseeing the earlier phases of the review. Below we briefly summarize the main concerns, our responses, and the corresponding revisions. All changes are highlighted in blue in the revised manuscript. 

**We also note that both reviewers who have responded to our rebuttal (iZkt and 9mCf) provided very positive comments on our response and the revised paper.** Reviewer iZkt explicitly stated that all concerns have been addressed and **has already increased the score**. Reviewer 9mCf stated that (at that time, we believe the score editing function was already closed) all concerns except W2 have been addressed, and requested further analysis of W2. We have responded and provided comprehensive theoretical justification and empirical evidence to specifically address W2.

---

### 1. Novelty and difference w.r.t. existing lifelong learning solvers [1,2], and experimental comparison with generalizable VRP solvers 



Reviewers (A4WR, ckwk, 9mCf, iZkt) asked us to clarify our novelty relative to [1] and [2], and to compare against their methods as well as recent generalizable neural VRP solvers. (This is the major concern of all reviewers. Both reviewers who have responded to our rebuttal (iZkt and 9mCf) explicitly state that this concern has been addressed by our further clarification and additional experimental studies.)

- We have clearly distinguished our **scenario** from [1,2]: in our work, tasks differ in both **distribution and scale**, arrive in a **random and unknown order**, instance generation is **uncontrollable**, and performance is evaluated **throughout** the lifelong process. In contrast, [1,2] assume a fixed known task order, shared distributions/scales and controllable instance generation, and primarily evaluate only at the end of training.
- We have clarified the **methodological novelty**: step-based experiences (⟨state, behavior⟩), buffer-based behavior consolidation on **previous tasks**, reuse of buffered experiences instead of generating new ones, and a confidence-based weighting scheme combined with an RKLD-based decision-seeking objective.
- We have implemented and adapted the methods of [1] and [2] (no official code is available) to our scenarios via instance buffers. **We have added comprehensive experimental comparisons with their methods. Across CVRP and TSP and all task orders, LLR-BC achieves substantially better overall performance.**
- Beyond our original comparison with Omni (a recent meta-learning solver) and INViT (a recent and strong generalizable solver) in the lifelong setting, **we further added comparisons with INViT without lifelong mechanisms, as well as with two multi-task POMO variants (POMO-MT-EL/BL). LLR-BC matches or outperforms these baselines, highlighting both the benefit of lifelong learning and the effectiveness of LLR-BC.**

[1] Jingwen Li, et al. Enhancing the cross-size generalization for solving vehicle routing problems via continual learning, 2024. https://openreview.net/forum?id=WdvT2UgsTK.

[2] Shaodi Feng, et al. Lifelong learner: Discovering versatile neural solvers for vehicle routing problems, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.11679.


### 2. Experience buffer design

Reviewers (ckwk, 9mCf, iZkt) asked for motivation clarification and analysis of our buffer design, in particular: buffering experiences only in the final epoch of each task, and using step-level rather than instance-based experiences. (Again, both reviewers who have responded explicitly state that this concern has been addressed.)

We revised the paper to emphasize the design motivations (i.e., getting high-quality behaviors and increasing instance diversity of the buffer) and added the following ablation studies for further investigation:
  - **Buffer timing:** LLR-BC-EE (buffer at every epoch) performs noticeably worse, confirming the effectiveness of our design.
  - **State-based vs instance-based buffer:** LLR-BC-IB (instance-based experiences) performs noticeably worse, supporting our step-based design.
  - **Buffer diversity:** We measured the task diversity in the buffer and introduced a rescaled variant (LLR-BC-Res) with more balanced task frequencies. Its worse performance supports our original design.

### 3. Writing and reporting improvements

Finally, we:
- Proofread, corrected typos and improved explanations of reservoir sampling, KLD vs RKLD, and notation of figures.
- Added tables reporting **absolute solution distances and optimality gaps** on each task for all methods (Appendix D), addressing concerns about practical performance.

---

### Summary

Overall, we believe our further clarification and additional experimental studies successfully addressed all the concerns of reviewers. These revisions substantially strengthen the technical clarity, empirical support, and presentation of our work. 

Sincerely, 

Paper 11068 Authors
